yc_seed.long_description:
Infisical is the all-in-one security infrastructure platform for secrets, certificates, and privileged access management.

Infisical stores your secrets and injects them back into your development workflow, CI/CD pipelines, and cloud infrastructure. It comes with secrets versioning, point-in-time recovery, audit logging, automatic secret rotation capabilities, and more.
yc_seed.one_liner: Unified platform for secrets, certs, and privileged access management

scenario.description: A developer infrastructure platform for centrally storing and distributing sensitive configuration values — credentials, API keys, connection strings, and certificates — across a team's applications, environments, and CI/CD pipelines. It supports versioning, point-in-time recovery, audit logging, and automatic rotation, and is offered both as a managed cloud service and as a self-hosted deployment for compliance-conscious customers who run it on their own infrastructure.

repository.name: Infisical/infisical
repository.description: Primary monorepo containing the web dashboard, the main Node.js API backend, a newer partial Go backend rewrite, CLI, Helm charts, and Docker/Docker Compose deployment configs.
repository.readme: Describes Infisical as an open-source security infrastructure platform for secrets, certificate (PKI), and privileged access management. Covers a dashboard for managing secrets across environments with versioning and rotation, internal/external certificate authority support, a key management system, and just-in-time privileged access with session recording. Documents SDKs for Node, Python, Go, Ruby, Java, and .NET, a CLI, and a REST API, with both a managed cloud offering and self-hosted deployment via Docker/Docker Compose/Kubernetes. The README itself does not enumerate the internal database or backend framework choices, deferring to the deployment docs.
repository.license_notes: Open-core licensing: the repository's root LICENSE file states that all content is MIT ('MIT Expat') except anything under an 'ee/' directory, which is covered by a separate proprietary 'Infisical Enterprise License' (found at backend/src/ee/LICENSE.md) that restricts production use of those enterprise features to paying subscribers, though modification for development/testing is permitted.

clients.description: Web dashboard used to manage secrets, certificates, access policies, and privileged sessions. Built with React 18, Vite as the build tool, TanStack Query/Router for data fetching and routing, Zustand for state, Radix UI/Tailwind CSS for the component layer, and React Hook Form with Zod for form validation.

backends.description: Primary API server handling secrets, certificate/PKI operations, privileged access management, auth, third-party integrations, and background jobs. Uses Knex.js as its SQL query builder against PostgreSQL, ioredis/BullMQ for Redis-backed sessions and job queues, and Zod for runtime validation.

Newer, partial rewrite of portions of the Node.js backend (auth, permissions, KMS/HSM crypto operations, and parts of the secrets-manager API) using the chi router, oapi-codegen, and raw pgx queries against the same PostgreSQL database, plus its own Redis client. The repository's own contributor-facing documentation for this directory describes it as an in-progress migration of parts of the Node backend to Go.

databases.name: PostgreSQL
databases.description: Sole primary datastore for all application data — secrets, certificates, users, projects, access policies, and (by default) audit logs — queried via Knex.js from the Node backend and via pgx from the Go backend. Infisical's own self-hosting docs state PostgreSQL is the only database it supports, recommending version 16 and requiring 14+.

hosting.description: Infisical Cloud runs Multi-AZ, encrypted RDS PostgreSQL instances (one for core application data, a separate one for license management) per its published cloud architecture docs; self-hosted deployments run their own PostgreSQL 14+ instance.

justifications.reason: Moved from MongoDB to PostgreSQL primarily to serve self-hosted, compliance-focused customers better: relational features like transactions and CASCADE deletes removed a class of orphaned-data bugs, and standard PostgreSQL is far easier for customers to deploy and operate on any cloud than a clustered MongoDB setup.
justifications.evidence: Infisical's engineering blog post on the migration says the schemaless MongoDB design caused inconsistent versioning and cleanup issues, and that self-hosting customers struggled to deploy and scale MongoDB compared to SQL databases; a companion announcement post adds that MongoDB's post-SSPL relicensing left many cloud providers offering only outdated managed MongoDB versions, further complicating self-hosting.

justifications.reason: PostgreSQL was chosen over MongoDB and over alternative ORMs/query builders (Drizzle, Prisma, TypeORM were evaluated) for its broad community support, universal availability as a managed service across cloud providers, and native relational modeling; Knex.js was selected as the query builder for fine-grained control paired with TypeScript and Zod validation.
justifications.evidence: The technical migration write-up describes evaluating Drizzle, Prisma, TypeORM, and Knex.js before settling on Knex for granular control and TypeScript integration, and states the switch removed inefficient aggregation/$lookup simulations, contributing to roughly a 50% database cost reduction.

migration_history.reason: Growing self-hosted, compliance-driven adoption exposed MongoDB's lack of transactions/cascading cleanup (causing orphaned data), operational complexity for self-hosting customers versus SQL databases, and reduced availability of current managed MongoDB versions from cloud providers after its SSPL relicensing.
migration_history.evidence: The migration took roughly 3-4 months including planning and rewrite. Engineers used Knex.js as the new query builder and a temporary LevelDB key-value store to map MongoDB ObjectIds (including recursive folder hierarchies) to new PostgreSQL identifiers. Production cutover ran during a 6-hour read-only window covering millions of records with zero reported data loss, and the first PostgreSQL-backed release was tagged infisical/v0.46.11-postgres on Feb 29, 2024. A public migration guide walks self-hosted operators through the same process using MIGRATION_MODE, mongodump/mongorestore, and pg_dump/pg_restore; support for the MongoDB-backed releases ended entirely after a two-month grace period.

databases.name: Redis
databases.description: Used as more than a cache: it backs the background job queue (BullMQ in the Node backend), distributed locks, cross-instance coordination for scheduled jobs, session storage, and rate-limit counters. Infisical's own hardware-requirements docs warn operators to configure a non-evicting cache policy and enable persistence because losing this data means losing queued work, not just a cache miss.

hosting.description: Infisical Cloud runs managed Redis 7 ElastiCache clusters (separate clusters for the core app and the license service) per its published cloud architecture docs; self-hosted deployments run their own standalone Redis 6.x/7.x instance (Redis Cluster mode is not supported).

justifications.reason: Redis was adopted as required infrastructure (not optional) because the backend relies on it for job-queue durability, distributed locking/coordination across instances, and rate limiting, in addition to session caching.
justifications.evidence: The self-hosting hardware requirements page explains that Redis stores the background job queue, distributed locks, cross-instance coordination state for scheduled jobs, and rate-limit counters, and instructs operators to treat its availability requirements the same as Infisical's own instances since it is a single point of failure.
